stories.title: Japan's MMX mission is days from launch to bring back a piece of Phobos
paragraphs: Japan's space agency JAXA is preparing to launch its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which aims to work out where Mars' two moons, Phobos and Deimos, came from and to deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. According to a NASA release dated Oct. 15, the spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA's Tanegashima Space Center at 12:41 p.m. PT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. Japan time on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

NASA says the moons' origin has long been debated. "Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters.

NASA's contributions include the MEGANE spectrograph, built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, which measures neutrons and gamma rays from the surface of Phobos to determine its chemical makeup. NASA is also supplying a pneumatic sampler mounted on one of the landing legs, developed by Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, which gathers surface material with bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas. JAXA's own C-Sampler will take cores from a few inches deeper.

According to NASA, the spacecraft will arrive at Mars in August 2027, collect its Phobos sample no earlier than December 2028, and deliver it to Earth in 2031. NASA will receive and curate about 15% of the returned sample at Johnson Space Center in Houston.

stories.title: China drafts export controls on frontier AI models, with a fast track for open weights
paragraphs: China's commerce and science ministries have released a draft update to the country's catalog of banned and restricted export technologies that targets 23 key AI technologies across large models, agents, compute clusters and data processing, The Decoder reported on Oct. 16. According to the report, AI tools that can write or alter malware on their own to attack critical infrastructure, the military or government agencies would face a total export ban, while certain AI tools for finding software vulnerabilities would face new export limits.

The Decoder reports that the core technologies behind large models, including weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture and training methods, would be controlled once a model reaches 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, has at least 2 trillion parameters, or ranks in the global top 10 on public rankings. Models trained on China's legally defined "important data" would also be covered, with lawfully public data exempt.

At the same time, the draft creates a fast track: according to The Decoder, publishing restricted AI technology and weights as open source qualifies for "automatic licensing," cleared as soon as a company files the paperwork. AI technology that is already public is exempt, and using restricted models through APIs, apps or websites stays outside the controls, while installing them on local servers abroad would need a standard export license. Until the final rules take effect, companies must register affected exports through the commerce ministry's portal.

stories.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight model
paragraphs: Meta released Muse Spark Open on Oct. 15, the open-weight version of its Muse Spark model, and calls it the "most capable US open-weight model to date," The Verge and The Decoder reported. According to MarkTechPost, it is a mixture-of-experts model with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active per token, a context window of 1 million tokens, and support for text, image, video and audio input with text output.

Meta says the model can run on a desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with Apple's MLX framework, and The Verge reports the two companies worked together on the launch. On Meta's own comparison, MarkTechPost notes the model leads on the MCP-Atlas tool-use benchmark with 89.2, but trails Kimi K3, GLM 5.3 and Qwen3.8 on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 coding test, scoring 76.4. The Decoder reports it still falls well short of Meta's paid Muse Wonder Full models.

The weights are on Hugging Face. According to The Decoder and MarkTechPost, the Muse Model License permits use, fine-tuning and redistribution, requires the label "Built with Muse Spark Open," and requires a separate agreement with Meta for providers earning more than $20 million a year who offer the model as an API service.

stories.title: USC scientists grow a renewable supply of engineered cancer-fighting immune cells
paragraphs: Researchers led by the University of Southern California report a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells for cancer treatment, in a study published in the journal Cell, according to a USC release carried by ScienceDaily on Oct. 16. The team worked with granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs), immature cells that normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells.

The researchers developed a defined chemical mixture that let GMPs survive and multiply for long periods in the lab without maturing, while keeping their ability to become functional macrophages. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew," said corresponding author Qi-Long Ying of the Keck School of Medicine of USC. A lab at Stanford led by Ravi Majeti independently showed the cells could be maintained and genetically engineered.

The team engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that targets a cancer marker. In mice, the cells settled in the bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors, with stronger effects when an added immune-activating signal was included. The release notes the cancer results are preclinical and that more research is needed to show whether the approach is safe and effective in people.

sources.name: ScienceDaily (Keck School of Medicine of USC)

stories.title: A 'golden tree' coral off Costa Rica gets a new family on the tree of life
paragraphs: Researchers led by Odalisca Breedy of the University of Costa Rica have described a deep-sea octocoral so unusual that it needed a new family, ScienceAlert reported on Oct. 16. They named it Laurinque elenya, from Tolkien's Elvish language Quenya, meaning "golden tree of the stars." It was found on a seamount off Costa Rica at depths of 360 to 529 meters (about 1,181 to 1,735 feet) during dives with the underwater vehicle SuBastian in 2019 and 2023.

According to ScienceAlert, the colonies can grow more than a meter tall and 1.2 meters wide, with dense branches covered in unusually long polyps. Two genetic markers pointed to two different octocoral families, so the team collected new specimens and analyzed hundreds of genetic regions. That showed the coral is closely related to the family Eunicellidae but distinct from it, making it the first known member of a new family, Laurinqueidae.

The coral gardens grow in water with extremely low oxygen at 8 to 11 degrees Celsius (46 to 52 degrees Fahrenheit), above a seafloor almost covered by pink brittle stars, ScienceAlert reports. The researchers report possible sightings off Panama and the Galápagos Islands, which have not yet been confirmed.
